newsitem.title: USA: Two tax breaks proposed for U.S. farmers.
newsitem.headline: Two tax breaks proposed for U.S. farmers.

text.p: U.S. farmers, who enjoyed high prices and large crops this year, need two tax breaks to avoid a potentially large tax bite so they will have the cash to weather bad years, farm-state lawmakers said Thursday.
They pledged to press for speedy passage of an exemption that would allow farmers to use commodity contracts to defer income into the next tax year.
Concern is high in farm country that the Internal Revenue Service will change the rules on use of so-called forward contracts, a popular merchandising tool.
Bills were pending in the House and Senate to exempt forward contracts from being counted when the alternate minimum tax is calculated.

In a separate step, lawmakers announced that companion bills would be filed in the House and Senate to allow farmers to average the income over two years so they would not be penalized for a good year.
Income-averaging would "give farmers some additional flexibility" in managing their cash, the measure's sponsor, Michigan Republican Representative Nick Smith, said.

Farmer fears of big tax bills have been fanned for months thanks to a recent IRS ruling involving a potato farmer, who must pay alternative minimum tax on income from a forward contract in the year when it was signed, not when the money was received.
Forward contracts are a way for farmers to "lock in" favorable prices but also can be used as a way to even out income.
"People are very concerned about this situation out there and they should be," said Representative Bill Barrett, Nebraska Republican.
He described how one farmer in his area might face a tax bill of $32,000, which would slightly exceed his income, if he had to include a $100,000 sale under a forward contract.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin has defended the IRS decision on the potato farmer but said last month that he would support efforts in Congress to change the law.
